report:
Conclusion: the claim is well supported. The adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix) reduces shingles in adults ≥70, though protection is somewhat lower than in ages 50–69 and requires two doses.

The pivotal ZOE-70 randomized, placebo-controlled trial in adults ≥70 concluded that the glycoprotein-E/AS01B subunit vaccine “reduce[d] the risks of herpes zoster and postherpetic neuralgia” in this age group (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1603800; abstract: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27626517/). CDC summarizes the clinical evidence as about 91% effectiveness against shingles in adults ≥70 after the full series, versus 97% in healthy adults 50–69 (https://www.cdc.gov/shingles/vaccines/index.html). FDA labeling likewise approves Shingrix for prevention of herpes zoster in adults ≥50 and reports efficacy results specifically for subjects ≥70 (https://www.fda.gov/media/108597/download).

Caveats: efficacy is not 100%; reactogenicity (injection-site pain, fatigue, myalgia) is common but usually short-lived; and evidence in frail or immunocompromised patients is more nuanced, though RZV is non-live and is recommended for many immunocompromised adults. Overall, for community-dwelling adults ≥70 able to receive two doses, the evidence strongly supports substantial reduction in shingles and related complications.
